system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

1. Obstructive sleep apnea.
2. Morbid obesity.

Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
Discharge Instructions: Please call your surgeon or return to 
the emergency department if you develop a fever greater than 
101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, 
pain unrelieved by your pain medication, severe nausea or 
vomiting, severe abdominal bloating, inability to eat or drink, 
foul smelling or colorful drainage from your incisions, redness 
or swelling around your incisions, or any other symptoms which 
are concerning to you.

Diet: Stay on Stage III diet until your follow up appointment. 
Do not self advance
diet, do not drink out of a straw or chew gum.

Medication Instructions:
Resume your home medications, CRUSH ALL PILLS.
You will be starting some new medications:
1.  You are being discharged on medications to treat the pain 
from your operation. These medications will make you drowsy and 
impair your ability to drive a motor vehicle or operate 
machinery safely. You MUST refrain from such activities while 
taking these medications.
2. You should begin taking a chewable complete multivitamin with 
minerals. No gummy vitamins.
3. You will be taking Zantac liquid ___ mg twice daily for one 
month. This medicine prevents gastric reflux.
4. You will be taking Actigall 300 mg twice daily for 6 months. 
This medicine prevents you from having problems with your 
gallbladder.
5. You should take a stool softener, Colace, twice daily for 
constipation as needed, or until you resume a normal bowel 
pattern.
6. You must not use NSAIDS (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory 
drugs) Examples are Ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, Nuprin and 
Naproxen. These agents will cause bleeding and ulcers in your 
digestive system.

Activity:
No heavy lifting of items ___ pounds for 6 weeks. You may 
resume moderate
exercise at your discretion, no abdominal exercises.

Wound Care:
You may shower, no tub baths or swimming. 
If there is clear drainage from your incisions, cover with 
clean, dry gauze. 
Your steri-strips will fall off on their own. Please remove any 
remaining strips ___ days after surgery.
Please call the doctor if you have increased pain, swelling, 
redness, or drainage from the incision sites. 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ woman with morbid obesity and esophageal dysmotility,
status post gastric bypass.

SINGLE CONTRAST UPPER GI SERIES:  Scout views demonstrate no free air under
the diaphragm.  A drain is noted within the left upper quadrant.  Surgical
clips are seen along the left mid abdomen.  Due to table restrictions related
to weight, the exam was performed only in the upright position.  Water-soluble
contrast followed by thin barium was used in the study.  Contrast was noted to
pass freely through the esophagus filling the included portion of the stomach
with prompt emptying into the jejunum at the site of gastrojejunal
anastomosis.  There is no evidence of dehiscence or escape of barium into the
excluded stomach.

IMPRESSION:  Status post gastric bypass with no evidence of obstruction or
leak. Findings discussed with ___ at 11:21pm on ___.

diagnoses.long_title: Body Mass Index 40 and over, adult

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. __ from the surgery team. You’re here for your planned gastric bypass—how are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous, mostly. I’ve tried diets so many times and I’m scared about surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’ll walk you through each step. The plan is a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and we’ll also do an endoscopy during the operation to check everything from the inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will this help my reflux and sleep apnea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weight loss after bypass often improves reflux symptoms and can improve obstructive sleep apnea over time. We’ll still have you use your CPAP as usual right now, especially while you’re recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I brought my CPAP. Should I use it tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—please do. We’ll also monitor your breathing closely after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take citalopram and Abilify. Do I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we plan to resume your home medications after surgery, but for now and after discharge you’ll need to crush pills so they go down safely while your new connection heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Crush all of them? Even Protonix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—crush all pills. For Protonix specifically, you can crush it and mix it in something like yogurt as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What are the biggest risks I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the hospital we watch for bleeding, infection, and problems at the new connections like a leak or blockage. After discharge, we’ll review warning signs—fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe belly pain, vomiting, or drainage/redness at the incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And pain—how bad is it usually?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right after surgery we typically use a Dilaudid PCA so you can control pain safely. As you improve, we switch to oral pain medicine like Roxicet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to head to the operating room. Any last questions before we get started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just… please tell me if everything goes okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We will. We’ll update you after you’re awake in recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in the recovery area now. The laparoscopic gastric bypass and the endoscopy are done, and everything went smoothly. Your blood pressure and heart rate have been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m really sleepy. My stomach hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected right after surgery. You have the Dilaudid PCA—press the button when you need it. We’ll keep checking your pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel tight in my belly. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—some tightness and soreness around the small port sites is normal. We also placed a JP drain to collect any fluid; we’ll monitor the output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I drink water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet tonight. Tomorrow we’ll do an upper GI study to confirm there’s no leak, and then we’ll start you on the first stage of the post-bypass diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any nausea or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little nauseous, but not throwing up. I used my CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on CPAP at night. Today’s main step is the upper GI imaging study to check the new connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens during that test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll drink contrast while they take X-ray images. We’re looking to make sure contrast goes through the new pathway and that there’s no leak or obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your upper GI study looks good—no evidence of obstruction or leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So I can start drinking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start Stage 1 diet today and advance slowly as you tolerate it. Small sips, no straws, and no chewing gum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why no straws?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Straws can make you swallow extra air, which can cause painful bloating and discomfort while you’re healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is better but the PCA makes me groggy. Can I switch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—since you’re tolerating liquids and doing well, we can transition from the Dilaudid PCA to oral Roxicet for pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about constipation from pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. We’ll use a stool softener like Colace, and we’ll encourage walking, which also helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have you been able to get up and walk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I walked in the hallway. It hurts a bit when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal early on. Keep doing short walks—walking helps prevent complications and speeds recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re progressing well. How are you doing with the diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m sipping okay. I’m scared to drink too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That caution is good. Take small, frequent sips. We’ve advanced you gradually, and the goal is to be on Stage III diet by discharge and stay there until your follow-up—don’t self-advance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When does the drain come out? It’s uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check the output and the sites. If everything looks appropriate, we can remove the JP drain today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your port sites look dry, and the drain output is minimal. We removed the JP drain without difficulty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That was quick. What should I watch for at the incisions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower, but no tub baths or swimming. If there’s clear drainage, cover with clean dry gauze. Call us for increasing pain, swelling, redness, or foul-smelling or colored drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take ibuprofen if I get sore at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, and naproxen. They can cause bleeding and ulcers after this surgery. Use the prescribed pain medication instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What medicines am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with Roxicet for pain as needed, Colace for constipation, Actigall twice daily to help prevent gallbladder problems, and Protonix twice daily—crushed and mixed as directed. You’ll also resume your home meds like citalopram, lorazepam as needed, and Abilify—also crushed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actigall—how long do I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For six months. It helps reduce the risk of gallbladder issues during rapid weight loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard something about vitamins. When do I start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start a chewable complete multivitamin with minerals—no gummy vitamins. That’s important after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about activity? I have kids at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for six weeks. You can do moderate exercise as you feel able, but avoid abdominal exercises. Keep walking daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with Dr. __ in about two weeks. Stay on Stage III diet until that appointment.
